clue.text: Studio boss reshaped Steinway lid with one cut

indicators.note: something reshaped has been given a new form, so the letters go into a new order
with one cut means a single item is taken away from the words before it

parts.note: the piano maker's name, taken as written
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I, which is removed

explanation.surface: A film studio chief takes a saw to the lid of a grand piano.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one I out of STEINWAY LID and rearrange the remaining ten letters to get WALT DISNEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Walt Disney founded and ran the famous animation studio, so he is the archetypal studio boss.

clue.text: Gastronome making fine wine, initially tasting of oak?

indicators.note: making one thing into another here means changing a letter of the gourmet's word

parts.note: a foody (or foodie) is a food lover
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine; this letter is swapped out

indicators.note: initially points to just the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of wine replaces it

explanation.surface: A food lover's wine has picked up an oaky flavour from the barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: In FOODY, change the F (fine) to W (wine, initially) to give WOODY. The question mark flags that woody is a wine-taster's description rather than a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine critics call a wine woody when barrel-ageing has given it the flavour of oak timber.

clue.text: Bluff English doctor fills quiet time

indicators.note: to fill something is to go inside it, so the first pair sits within the later phrase

parts.note: a lull is a quiet spell
standard abbreviation
a general practitioner

explanation.surface: A blunt English GP takes up a slack period in the surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bluff' looks like an adjective (blunt), but here it is the noun for a deception.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg-pull is a joke or hoax played on someone, just as a bluff is a pretence meant to deceive.

clue.text: Grounds invaded by Nazis wearing bandages

indicators.note: an invaded territory has a force inside it, so the later letters go into the first word

parts.note: grounds are the sediment, as in coffee grounds
the Nazi paramilitary force
you are in a garment when you wear it

explanation.surface: A wartime scene: territory overrun by Nazi troops wrapped in bandages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' suggests land to be invaded, but it means sediment.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressings are the coverings put on wounds, which is what bandages are.

clue.text: Weaponised rocket NASA modestly keeps under wraps

indicators.note: something kept under wraps is concealed inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: The space agency quietly keeps a military missile project secret.
explanation.definitionFit: SAM stands for surface-to-air missile, a rocket built as a weapon.

clue.text: Principle by which kitchen's contents are organised

indicators.note: organised means put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged
the contents of a word are everything except its first and last letters

parts.note: kitchen without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A tidy cook explains the rule behind how the kitchen cupboards are arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a moral principle or set of values that guides conduct.

clue.text: Sound of sheep entertains our ears regularly in Australian bush

indicators.note: a host entertains guests indoors, so the first word holds the selected letters

parts.note: the bleat of a sheep

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, every other one

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Out in the Australian outback, bleating sheep keep filling our ears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound of sheep' is just BAA, not a sound-alike device. Bauera is a less familiar plant name, so the wordplay does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Bauera is a genus of flowering shrubs native to eastern Australia, so it is a bush found there.

clue.text: Thug whose cap has come off uses extra clips

indicators.note: a word losing its cap loses its top, which in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: a lout is a boorish thug
as in takes the bus

explanation.surface: A hooligan who has lost his hat helps himself to more cuttings.
explanation.definitionFit: Out-takes are filmed scenes left out of the final cut, often shown afterwards as extra footage.

clue.text: No good opening new Merlot for ages

indicators.note: opening something up lets another piece sit in the gap made inside it
something new has been remade, so the wine's letters come out in a fresh order

parts.note: the grape variety, taken as written
NG is the standard abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: Uncorking a fresh bottle of Merlot early is a mistake when it should be laid down for years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' reads like uncorking a bottle, but it means NG goes into the middle of the rearranged wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-term describes something that lasts or applies over a lengthy period, which is what for ages expresses.

clue.text: American after great success takes a break

indicators.note: after places the American piece behind the rest
to take something in is to hold it, so the success word swallows the small article

parts.note: a hit is a big success
taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Fresh from a triumph, an American goes on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only 'break'; 'takes a' does double duty in the wordplay. Read as a noun, 'break' is a pause.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiatus is a pause or gap in an activity, the same as a break.

clue.text: Apothecary's back in Tottenham returning sickly potions

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way it went, so the team name runs right to left
in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: Tottenham Hotspur football club is known as Spurs

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of apothecary

explanation.surface: A chemist from north London brings back over-sweet medicines.
explanation.walkthrough: The Y is from the back of apothecary and goes inside the reversed SPURS, after its first letter. Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club, nicknamed Spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Syrups are thick sweet liquids, and medicinal syrups are cloyingly sugary potions.

clue.text: Stream Alien and Troy for writer whose plots can lack thrills

definitions.text: writer whose plots can lack thrills

parts.note: a beck is a northern English word for a brook
the extraterrestrial of the film
t is the abbreviation for troy, the weight system

explanation.surface: A list of films (a river, an alien and an epic of Troy) for a writer who prefers slow stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Troy is not the city but troy weight, abbreviated t. Samuel Beckett's 'Waiting for Godot' is famous as a play in which nothing happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Beckett wrote plays whose plots are notoriously eventless, such as Waiting for Godot.

clue.text: PM a follower of N Armstwong?

indicators.note: the lisping spelling of the astronaut's surname shows that an R is to be said as a W

parts.note: Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon after Neil Armstrong; B Aldrin is his name with initial

explanation.surface: A comic baby-talk question about who came after the first man on the Moon.
explanation.walkthrough: B ALDRIN, the second man on the Moon, said with the clue's R-to-W lisp gives BALDWIN. Stanley Baldwin was a British Prime Minister between the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Baldwin served three times as British Prime Minister, so he is a PM.

clue.text: 'King promoter' once, all shook up?

parts.note: surface reading: someone who once championed a monarch, perhaps a royalist agitator
setter's reading: All Shook Up is an Elvis Presley hit, and the King is Elvis, so this is the manager who promoted him

explanation.walkthrough: Elvis Presley was known as the King, and All Shook Up was one of his number ones; his notorious manager was Colonel Tom Parker.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Tom Parker managed and promoted Elvis Presley, the King of rock and roll, throughout his career.

clue.text: Children creep home for toast

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for children
to inch is to creep slowly forward
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: Children tiptoe back to the house to find something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toast' suggests bread, but it is the drinking salute.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned informal toast said when raising glasses, like cheers.

clue.text: Acknowledgement of man whose parts are scattered around here

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an expression of gratitude

definitions.text: man whose parts are scattered around here
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the actor ..., whose film roles are dotted around this grid

explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' are acting roles: Tom Hanks played Woody, Walt Disney, Captain Phillips, Sully, Captain Miller, Andrew Beckett and Colonel Tom Parker, all answers here. T HANKS reads as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thanks is a word of gratitude, an acknowledgement of a favour; the actor's initial and surname make the same letters.

clue.text: See 12
Many stars Greek character spots in the audience

parts.note: the Greek letter pi

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so it is the spoken form that counts

parts.note: to spot is to see

explanation.surface: Someone notices a Greek performer among the spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, PI plus 'sees' sounds like the constellation's name, pronounced pie-seez.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisces is a zodiac constellation, a group of many stars forming the shape of two fish.

clue.text: Dome-shaped top, going on Pepsi bottles?

indicators.note: bottles as a verb means holds inside, so the drink word encloses the other piece

parts.note: Pepsi is a brand of cola
as in what's up, meaning what's going on

explanation.surface: A rounded cap screwed onto Pepsi bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' looks like the noun, but it is the verb for holding something inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupola is a small domed structure crowning a roof, so a dome-shaped top to a building.

clue.text: Australian wildlife cut back, out of your tree

indicators.note: going back means travelling right to left through the word for cut

parts.note: to mow is to cut grass
bats is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Australia's native animals are being cut back by someone who must be mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of your tree' feels like the wildlife's home, but it is slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Wombats are burrowing marsupials native to Australia, an example of its wildlife.

clue.text: Don't drink six-pack you shouldn't have at home

parts.note: a six-pack is a set of well-defined abdominal muscles
ta is British informal for thanks, what you say on receiving a gift
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Advice to someone who keeps a six-pack of beer in the house: leave it alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six-pack' suggests beer cans, but it is the stomach muscles. 'You shouldn't have' is said on receiving a present, so it means thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from something, most often from drinking alcohol.

clue.text: US cop likely to punch murderer

indicators.note: a punch drives into its target, so the first word goes inside the second

parts.note: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis
apt to means likely to

explanation.surface: An American police officer is expected to throw a punch at a killer.
explanation.definitionFit: In US police forces a captain is a senior rank, so a captain is a police officer.

clue.text: Cost of borrowing one pound for thirty days

parts.note: annual percentage rate, the quoted cost of a loan
Roman numeral one
L is the abbreviation for the pound (libra)

explanation.surface: A lender quotes the interest charged on a one-pound loan for a month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thirty days' sounds like a loan term but is the month itself, from the rhyme 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November'.
explanation.definitionFit: April is one of the months with exactly thirty days, so thirty days can describe it.

clue.text: Idiot seconds from time essentially steers ball to goalscorer

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: seconds from a run of words means taking the letter in position two of each

parts.note: the second letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A football pundit fumes as a fool, deep into stoppage time, sets up a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds' and 'time' read like a match clock, but 'seconds from' means second letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In football an assist is the pass that sets up a teammate to score a goal.

clue.text: Small ravine, less grand defile

parts.note: standard abbreviation

indicators.note: less means without, so one letter is taken away from the ravine word

parts.note: a gully is a narrow ravine
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A little gorge, not very impressive, forms a narrow mountain pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defile' wants to be a noun, a narrow pass that fits the ravine scene; here it is the verb meaning to soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To sully is to stain or tarnish, especially a reputation, which is to defile it.

clue.text: Food processor that's miles worse

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for miles
iller means more ill, so worse

explanation.surface: A kitchen appliance review: this blender is far inferior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food processor' suggests a kitchen gadget, but it is a person who processes grain.
explanation.definitionFit: A miller grinds grain into flour, so he processes food on an industrial scale.

clue.text: Attractive plastic bell outside budget furniture store

indicators.note: outside means wrapped around, so the shop sits within the rearranged letters
plastic material can be moulded into any shape, so the letters are remoulded

parts.note: taken as written
the Swedish flat-pack furniture chain

explanation.surface: A cheap plastic bell hangs outside the door of a discount furniture shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic' looks like the bell's material, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Likeable means pleasant and easy to like, so attractive in personality.

clue.text: Batter shelled scallops

indicators.note: shelled means stripped of its outer casing, so only the inner letters remain

parts.note: scallops are taken loosely as clams, a word whose inner letters are kept

explanation.surface: A cook coats shelled scallops in batter.
explanation.walkthrough: Scallops stand for CLAMS, both bivalve shellfish; remove the outside letters to leave the answer. 'Batter' is the verb to beat, not the coating.
explanation.definitionFit: To lam is an informal verb meaning to beat or thrash, the same as to batter.

clue.text: Slivovitz maybe, straight up, then ready for bed

parts.note: plumb means exactly vertical
randy means amorous, keen for sex

explanation.surface: A nightcap of Balkan spirit taken neat, and then off to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straight up' sounds like a drink served without ice, but it means vertical; 'ready for bed' is not sleepy but amorous.
explanation.definitionFit: Slivovitz is an Eastern European spirit distilled from plums, so it is an example of the drink.
